strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important failure mode: across five strong VLMs, errors on modified familiar objects frequently coincide with canonical counts rather than the visible content.
The evaluation is broad, covering seven domains, multiple image resolutions, two counting prompts, and both photorealistic and programmatically generated images.

The bias-aligned error analysis and the in-image-text, debiased-prompt, and double-check experiments are useful diagnostic probes. The appendix also documents dataset construction and prompts extensively.
The central descriptive observation—current VLMs perform poorly on subtle counterfactual visual changes—is striking and potentially valuable as a benchmark contribution.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is not established. Canonical answers after a counting failure do not show that memorized knowledge overrode perceived evidence: models may simply fail to resolve or count the relevant elements and then fall back on a reasonable prior. Matched unfamiliar-object controls, cropped/zoomed inputs, context removal, and perceptually matched non-counterfactual counting tasks are needed.

The unmodified-image sanity check is inadequate: it uses only 66 images rather than matched originals for the full benchmark, and canonical counts can themselves be answered from prior knowledge without inspecting the image. It therefore does not demonstrate that each counterfactual modification is perceptible under comparable conditions.

Benchmark validity is insufficiently established. There is no human accuracy study, inter-annotator agreement, or quantitative visibility criterion. Several logos are intentionally tiny—the manuscript itself asks readers to zoom in—and generated extra limbs may contain unnatural or fused geometry. These factors strongly confound bias with visual resolution and counting difficulty.

Several Q3 ground truths are semantically questionable. A flag with one altered stripe may still reasonably be called that country's flag, a modified Adidas-like mark may still be identified as Adidas, and a parametrically modified illusion can remain an instance of the same illusion family. Consequently, the reported below-chance Q3 accuracy is not reliably interpretable.

The statistical treatment is weak: models are sampled once at temperature 1, with no repeated runs, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or robustness analysis, despite multiple claims of significant differences. Two near-paraphrased prompts and three resized copies of each base image are correlated observations.

The claimed 1,392-image scale corresponds to only 464 underlying scenes before three-way resizing. Although resolution sensitivity motivates these copies, no results by resolution are reported. Feature size, modification direction, and other likely difficulty factors are also not analyzed.

The paper conflates memorized factual priors, generic contextual pattern completion, optical-illusion effects, and basic counting failures under the single term “bias.” In particular, failure on newly created patterned grids supports a general perception/localization limitation rather than the stated Internet-knowledge mechanism.

Novelty over existing counterfactual and visual-hallucination benchmarks is moderate, while presentation and reproducibility have notable gaps: the data/code URL is blank, the appendix's error-analysis section is unfinished, Gemini is inconsistently categorized as a thinking versus non-thinking model, and the claim of an improvement of “at most +2” conflicts with Table 5's +2.70 mean and +4.27 model-level improvement.

The evaluation spans seven visual domains and a broad collection of proprietary, open-source, reasoning, and pointing-capable models. The appendices provide substantial detail on prompts, model identifiers, generation procedures, and qualitative examples.
The large original-versus-counterfactual performance gap and concentration of predictions on canonical answers are interesting descriptive findings that merit further study.

The authors attempt numerous follow-up analyses, including multiple resolutions, repeated runs, prompting interventions, background alteration, in-image text, human evaluation, linear probing, tool use, and specialized counting models. The paper is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The central causal claim—that memorized knowledge overrides available visual evidence—is not established. Canonical errors can also arise from ordinary counting limitations, tiny targets, internal image downsampling, or response priors. The original-image sanity check is insufficient because canonical counts can be answered without inspecting the image; matched unfamiliar-object, text-only, no-image, and equal-difficulty perceptual controls are missing.

The Q3 evaluation is seriously confounded: every original has ground truth "Yes" and every counterfactual has ground truth "No," so the reported collapse cannot be separated from a generic yes-bias. Several labels are also semantically contestable: a four-stripe Adidas-like logo, altered national flag, or parametrically modified Ebbinghaus display may still reasonably be identified as an Adidas logo, that country's flag, or an Ebbinghaus illusion.

The background-removal experiment does not isolate background bias. It crops or segments targets, enlarges their effective scale, removes clutter, and for abstract tasks creates substantially different renderings that expose only the elements to count. The resulting gain therefore cannot be causally attributed to background semantic cues. Likewise, the in-image-text study lacks an irrelevant-text control.

Several headline mechanistic claims rely on observational correlations. Reasoning length is chosen by the model and confounded with item difficulty; sparse token bins and no controlled reasoning budgets, uncertainty estimates, or item-level regression do not support the claim that overthinking harms accuracy. Tool use, self-reported confidence, and two within-family size comparisons similarly do not justify claims about overconfidence or inverse scaling.

The stated scale is misleading: the 1,392 images comprise only 464 base scenes repeated at three resolutions, and the claimed 4,176-image suite further counts transformations of the same scenes. Resolutions and paraphrased prompts are dependent observations, yet there are no unit-aware confidence intervals or significance tests. Most temperature-1 model results come from one run, while the human study covers only the animal domain.

The linear probe does not show that the language model overrides a correctly represented count. A supervised binary classifier can exploit generator or editing artifacts without counting, and the paper does not state whether source images, species, editing trials, and resized duplicates were grouped across train/test splits, leaving a substantial leakage risk.

Quality-control and reporting problems undermine confidence in the results. Manual image review has no independent annotators or agreement statistics, and some examples contain very small or visually ambiguous modifications. Figures 32 and 34 mark outputs such as 4 versus a displayed ground truth of 5, and 7 versus 11, as correct. The tool-analysis prose also alternates between matched-resolution and all-resolution baselines, producing incompatible improvements (+1.9 versus +4.83).

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: the abstract's code-and-data URL is blank, exact scoring/parsing procedures and several inference settings are omitted, and proprietary API evaluations lack access dates. Overall, the descriptive failure pattern is promising, but the benchmark does not yet support its principal causal and mechanistic conclusions at a top-tier-conference standard.
